title: Storing Labeled Data in Dictionaries
content:
What problem does this solve?
A hero has a name, health, and gold — three related facts. Parallel variables work at first, but a dictionary groups labeled data under one name: each stat has a key you read and update.

Basic syntax
  hero = {"name": "Mira", "health": 42, "gold": 10}
  hero["gold"]
  hero["health"] = 35

What actually happens
Curly braces build a dict. Keys are usually strings; values can be any type. hero["gold"] looks up a value; assignment with hero["gold"] = 7 updates that entry in place.

When this is useful
Model records with named fields — character stats, shop prices, quest flags — instead of juggling many separate variables.
concepts: A dict maps keys to values with {key: value} syntax
Keys are labels — health and gold stay attached to the same hero

examples.title: Hero stats dict
examples.explanation: Bracket lookup reads each labeled field for messages.

examples.title: Spend gold
examples.explanation: Assignment updates the gold entry inside the same dict.

common_mistakes: Forgetting quotes around string keys — name is a variable, "name" is the key
Using square brackets on a list but parentheses on a dict — dicts use {}
Typo in a key name causes KeyError

exercises.title: Predict after a gold update
exercises.prompt: Trace the gold change before you answer, then click Check.
exercises.failure_message: Start at 10, subtract 3, then read hero["gold"] — not the name or health fields.
hints: The print shows the updated gold value only.

exercises.title: Complete the dict literal
exercises.prompt: Build a hero dict with keys "name", "health", and "gold". Replace None with the correct key for the name field.
exercises.starter_code:
name = "Mira"
hp = 42
gold = 10
hero = {None: name, "health": hp, "gold": gold}
print(hero["name"])
hints: Dict keys that are strings need quotes.
The first key should be the string "name".
Use "name": name inside the curly braces.

exercises.title: Fix the key lookup
exercises.prompt:
This program should print 42 (Mira's health), but it crashes. Python treats health inside the brackets as a variable name, not a dict key.

Run to see the error, fix the lookup, then Check.
hints: Run first — the error points at the lookup line.
String keys need quotes inside the brackets.
Use hero["health"] to read the health entry.

tests.name: hero
tests.message: Look up a value from hero with hero["health"], not print(42) alone.

exercises.title: Build hero stats
exercises.prompt:
Write make_stats(name, hp, gold) that returns a dictionary with exactly these string keys:
- "name" → the name argument
- "health" → the hp argument
- "gold" → the gold argument

Return the dict — do not print. This structure will reappear in later lessons.
hints: Return a dict literal with three key: value pairs.
Map health to the hp parameter.
Return a dict literal — do not print.

tests.message: All three keys should match the arguments.
Zero gold is valid — every key still required.
Do not hardcode Mira — use the parameters.
Build the dict from parameters, not a fixed hero.
The health key must store the hp argument.

exercises.title: Can they afford the purchase?
exercises.prompt:
Write can_afford(stats, price) where stats is a dictionary from make_stats (with a "gold" key).

Return True when stats["gold"] is greater than or equal to price, otherwise False. Do not print or modify the dictionary.
exercises.success_message: You read labeled data from a dict and combined it with a comparison — the foundation for shops and stat screens.
hints: Compare that value to price with >=.
Do not hardcode prices — use the price parameter.

tests.message: Exactly enough gold should return True.
Not enough gold should return False.
Zero gold cannot afford a positive price.
Use stats["gold"], not a hardcoded check for one hero.
